articles.title: World News in Brief: West Bank demolitions accelerate, urgent support for Sudan,  Haiti diplacement, AI hub to boost gender equality
articles.summary: The situation in the occupied West Bank continues to deteriorate, the UN human rights office has said, pointing to the “mass destruction” of Palestinian villages and forcible transfer of residents in Msafer Yatta, South Hebron Hills.
articles.content:
In a call for an immediate halt to the demolitions, the UN Office, OHCHR, said that Israeli bulldozers demolished homes, farm buildings, water tanks and solar panels in the village of Jinba on Wednesday.

Tweet URL

“The forcible transfer of a civilian population from their land by an occupying power is a war crime,” said Ajith Sunghay, head of OHCHR in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

Ethnic cleansing fears grow

Three more villages in Msafer Yatta have already been “almost entirely” destroyed in September 2026, OHCHR said, highlighting fears of ethnic cleansing in the occupied Palestinian territory.

Overall, there are 12 villages in Msafer Yatta housing over 1,100 Palestinians, most of whom have owned and lived on the land for generations

Israeli demolitions of Palestinian homes and infrastructure have displaced 1,500 people in the occupied West Bank so far this year, according to the UN aid coordination office, OCHA.

Sudan needs urgent support as El Niño compounds food insecurity

Funding shortages are limiting UN efforts to aid communities in Sudan impacted by ongoing war and displacement – just as El Niño threatens to bring 30 to 40 per cent less rainfall than usual.

In an alert, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) warned of worsening food security, for farmers, pastoralists and fishing communities in regions largely reclaimed by Government forces, during the protracted war with former paramilitary allies, the RSF.

The agency has several ways of supporting the most vulnerable, such as vaccinating millions of livestock and providing goats to displaced women-headed households and mothers, so that children have a ready supply of nutritious milk.

Soundcloud

Boosting food supply

FAO’s Rein Paulsen said the agency’s response is focused on mitigating the impacts of rainfall loss and drought on livestock to maintain healthy herds.

“This is about ensuring that the body weight of animals are retained, that they’re vaccinated against the types of diseases that will compromise their health, that they have access to animal feed concentrate.”

Another successful ongoing project that’s brought investment returns of 30 to one involves purchasing drought-resistant seed for farmers. From an initial $17 million outlay, farmers produced sorghum crops worth more than $500 million.

This year, the agency needs $193 million to support its initiatives. It is currently only 23 per cent funded.

Haiti's displacement crisis spreading beyond capital, IOM warns

Haiti's displacement crisis is spreading beyond Port-au-Prince, with some of the sharpest increases now occurring in regions once considered relatively safe, according to new data released this week by the UN International Organization for Migration (IOM).

The latest assessment recorded nearly 1.5 million internally displaced people nationwide, with almost 80 per cent now outside the capital as violence spreads into other areas.

The steepest rise was in Artibonite department, where displacement grew by 16 per cent between May and August.

Once a refuge for families fleeing violence, parts of the department are now facing escalating insecurity themselves.

Mass displacement

Recent attacks in Kenscoff, near the capital, displaced more than 4,000 people, with homes burned and reports of kidnappings and deaths.

“Violence, displacement, food insecurity, forced returns and climate risks are all unfolding at the same time, placing enormous pressure on families and communities,” said Elise Verron, IOM's Senior Emergency Coordinator in Haiti.

With the Atlantic hurricane season underway, many displaced families are living in informal settlements or host communities with little capacity to withstand further shocks.

IOM is appealing for $60 million to reach 6.4 million people under its 2026 crisis response plan.

UN Women launches digital hub dedicated to gender equality

Tweet URL

UN Women on Friday launched a Digital, Innovation and AI Hub focused on its core remit: gender equality.

It brings together researchers, governments, technology companies and women’s rights organizations to help shape artificial intelligence (AI) in ways that benefit women and girls.

The launch comes as world leaders coalesce for the General Assembly’s 81st session, where AI is high on the agender – but women and girls remain largely absent from the debate, the UN agency said.

8 in 10 AI jobs held by men

According to UN Women, men hold nearly eight in 10 AI jobs and almost nine in 10 senior leadership positions shaping the technology.

“The artificial intelligence systems we build today will shape how we live and work tomorrow. If women are missing from their design and governance, we risk carrying the inequalities of the present into the future,” said UN Women Executive Director Sima Bahous.

A global analysis of 133 AI systems by the agency, found that 44 per cent showed gender bias.

Additionally, nearly one in four women human rights defenders, activists and journalists surveyed by UN Women reported experiencing AI-assisted online violence.

The hub will generate evidence on how emerging technologies affect women and girls, support Member States in developing gender-responsible digital and AI policies and work with technology companies to embed gender equality principles into technological design and governance.

“AI can deepen gender inequality or help overcome it. That is a human choice – and those choices are being made now by engineers, companies, investors and governments,” Ms. Bahous said.

“Equality is not only about representation. It is also about power,” she added.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the launch of a UN Women Digital, Innovation and AI Hub dedicated to promoting gender equality in AI technology. This initiative addresses significant gender disparities in AI employment and leadership, aims to reduce gender bias in AI systems, and supports policies for gender-responsible digital governance. The story presents a meaningful, broad-impact action with clear details and potential positive societal change, qualifying as inspiring good news.

articles.title: Australia urges global cooperation on climate, AI checks and international law
articles.summary: Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese underlined the need for countries to work together to address the climate crisis, emerging technologies such as AI, and the breakdown of international rules, at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
articles.content:
He said that cooperating on urgent challenges that confront every country, creating solutions that work for citizens and staying true to the UN’s founding purpose “remains the test of our time” which “we can and we must pass”.

The UN was established eight decades ago “from the ruins of war” by citizens and leaders who vowed to work together to prevent another global conflict, Mr. Albanese stressed.

Uniting nations

“We can seize and share and shape the opportunities this moment holds in the interests of our citizens. But we can only do it together,” he said.

Mr. Albanese insisted that “the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone, nor can it be subcontracted to the world’s richest companies or dictated by the pace of technology.”

He stressed that “shaping a secure, peaceful and prosperous world is a task for all of us”, which is why Australia is seeking a non-permanent seat on the UN Security Council for 2029-2030.

Promoting wider perspectives

If successful, “Australia will safeguard the rules that protect us all by upholding international law, including the UN Charter and the sovereignty of all States,” he said.

“We will amplify the voices of small States and middle powers to ensure a wider range of perspectives shape the Council's decisions.”

The Australian premier noted that the world is rapidly changing and new issues – including climate change, emerging technologies such as AI, and the breakdown of trust, civility and social cohesion – demand the full attention of the international community.

He also emphasized the need to “embrace” change and reform multilateralism.

Cooperation, not coercion

“As a middle power, Australia is showing leadership and working with others on fresh ideas to tackle the big issues now facing the world in our region,” the Prime Minister said.

He highlighted how his Government is “elevating relationships that help to build sovereign capability and offer nations sovereign choice free from coercion”.

That way, partners can address the “big issues” they face such as economic and energy security, development and transnational crime, among others.

Social media ban

Mr. Albanese also recalled that last year Australia instituted a social media ban for people under 16, following the campaign by grieving parents who addressed the General Assembly that turned into global action.

“Already, more than 20 countries are bringing in or have brought in age restrictions on social media,” he said, “and with the European community taking action, there are many more to come.”
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article highlights Australia's call for global cooperation on critical issues like climate change, AI regulation, and upholding international law, emphasizing multilateralism and inclusive governance. It also notes Australia's leadership in promoting social media age restrictions to protect youth, reflecting meaningful, broad-scale efforts to address pressing global challenges with tangible societal benefits.

articles.title: Movement from behind your gadget
articles.summary: The growth of online activism has given different colors in the movement agendas. There is a debate on how effective it is, and how it could complement each other.
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ September 2026 Spotlight series, “Protest in Democracy.” With this Spotlight, we seek to explore the many forms of protest, the tactics states use to delegitimize and suppress them, and the complex relationship between protest and democracy. You can support this coverage by donating here.

The growing popularity and expanding use of social media have influenced the ways people express themselves. While protests once involved taking to the streets with banners and chants, such activities can now be carried out in the virtual realm. Messages and slogans are now conveyed through hashtags, digital posters, or videos posted across various social media channels. Events such as the Arab Spring and the Occupy Movement have further reinforced the phenomenon of online protest.

Both of them are effective, no?

What is the difference between online and offline protests? According to anthropologist Yatun Sastramidjaja, writing for the University of Amsterdam, there is no significant difference between offline and online protest, other than the setting — the real world versus the virtual world. Despite this difference in location, both forms can mobilize crowds, voice opinions, and support one another. A protest that begins online can spill over into the streets, as seen with the Arab Spring and the Occupy Movement. Such online-initiated protests can also raise awareness of specific issues, subsequently leading to offline protests.

These online movements are compelling because they tap into modern cultural trends, such as memes, hashtags, posters, and online petitions. Well-executed campaigns often employ dedicated graphic designers to select specific colors and typefaces that convey underlying meaning, carefully tailored to the nature of the protest. These chosen visual elements are then applied consistently across all online platforms, including websites, social media channels, posters, and other communication media. In essence, the protest is treated much like a product brand, requiring a clear and powerful identity.

This approach is indeed effective for embedding a social movement in people's minds, reaching both those accustomed to participating in protests and those drawn to the specific issues raised or the branding created by the organizers. It also proves effective across diverse demographics with varying modes of self-expression. These online protests have successfully mobilized a wide range of groups, including K-Pop fans from all over the world.

K-Pop, especially its fandom, is cited here as a prime example of youth culture that exerts influence across various spheres. In Korea, it played a role in the ousting of President Yoon, while in other countries — including Indonesia — K-Pop fandoms have actively participated in protests addressing social and political issues. Interactions among K-Pop fans typically take place online (on platforms like X, Facebook, and TikTok); consequently, movements often begin as online protests, with some individuals subsequently taking to the streets alongside other demonstrators.

But then, there are some disadvantages.

Although online protest is gaining popularity — especially among young people — it also has several drawbacks. One of them is uneven internet connectivity.

In her book “Social Media and Politics in Southeast Asia,” Merlyna Lim notes that early studies of digital networks hailed them as a new space for democratic processes, as they could transcend country borders and ultimately spur participation and social movements. But nowadays, the current distribution of digital technology is uneven; consequently, even though it can transcend national borders, the individuals involved are still primarily those who already possess good access to digital technology. Lim stated:

I contend that, setting aside the issue of unequal access, digital networks are not egalitarian networks where citizens have equal opportunities to participate in public discourse. First and foremost, the internet is never inherently egalitarian. Instead, the structure of the internet exhibits the characteristics of a scale-free network—a network in which the degree distribution follows a power law.

This uneven distribution of connectivity will hinder civil society organizations seeking to recruit new members from demographics different from their existing base. Furthermore, existing echo chambers are made worse by internet algorithms that suggest topics based on a user's interests, creating a limiting environment. For instance, if you are interested in environmental activism, your inbox will be flooded with suggestions on similar topics, and you will likely not see other appeals for activism that might also interest you, since the algorithm has latched on to your response to environmental activism.

Another concern is the assumption that people who participate in online protests are not necessarily willing to take to the streets or remain consistently engaged with the issues raised. Many people participate in online activism because, aside from the ease of doing so (such as posting memes or online posters), they can also take shelter behind anonymity. This differs from actually taking to the streets, which carries a higher risk of clashes with security forces. In response to this, the Open Society Foundation (OSF) has the view that online protests attract young people who are engaging with social issues for the first time, and it is the first step on the ladder to offline activism.

It is undeniable that there are various shortcomings, but in this short article, OSF suggests that civil society organizations (CSOs) can develop long-term strategies by incorporating online movements to champion specific issues. This involves planning for both online and offline engagement, as well as facilitating a seamless transition between the two. In essence, CSOs must devise ways to sustain public interest so that those initially engaged online remain committed to the cause over the long term and are willing to participate in offline activities.

To address the disparity in internet access, CSOs must continue to conduct face-to-face educational sessions and discussions that reach individuals with poor internet connectivity. Ultimately, even if access remains unequal, both online and offline activism can contribute meaningfully to a movement and complement each other.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the positive impact of online activism as a complementary form of protest that broadens participation and awareness in social and political movements globally. It discusses how digital protests can mobilize diverse groups, including youth cultures like K-Pop fandoms, and how civil society organizations can strategically integrate online and offline activism to sustain engagement despite challenges like unequal internet access. This reflects meaningful progress in democratic participation and social advocacy with broad societal significance.
articles.personality_title: How online activism is changing protests around the world
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Protests used to happen mostly in the streets, with people chanting and holding banners. But now, with social media, many protests happen online using hashtags, videos, and digital posters. Famous movements like the Arab Spring and Occupy Movement showed how online actions can lead to real-world protests.

**What happened** – Experts say online and offline protests work similarly, just in different places—online or in person. Online protests use popular trends like memes and hashtags to spread messages. Groups like K-Pop fans have used online platforms to support causes and even join street protests. However, not everyone has good internet access, and some people only join online because it feels safer and easier.

**Impact** – Online activism helps reach many people, including young ones who might not join street protests at first. It can spread awareness quickly and connect different groups worldwide. But uneven internet access and online “echo chambers” can limit who joins and how much they stay involved. This means online protests alone are not enough but can support and grow real-world actions.

**What's next step** – Organizations working for social causes plan to mix online and offline protests. They want to keep people interested online and help them take part in street protests too. They also aim to reach people without good internet by holding face-to-face meetings. This combined approach can make movements stronger and more lasting.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Online protests add new ways for people to join causes and, when combined with in-person actions, help create bigger and more lasting movements worldwide.
articles.personality_title_fr: Comment l'activisme en ligne transforme les manifestations dans le monde
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les manifestations se déroulaient principalement dans la rue, avec des slogans et des pancartes. Aujourd'hui, grâce aux réseaux sociaux, beaucoup de manifestations ont lieu en ligne via des hashtags, des vidéos et des affiches numériques. Des mouvements célèbres comme le Printemps arabe et Occupy ont montré comment les actions en ligne peuvent déboucher sur des manifestations dans la rue.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Les experts expliquent que les manifestations en ligne et en personne fonctionnent de façon similaire, mais dans des lieux différents. Les protestations en ligne utilisent des tendances populaires comme les mèmes et les hashtags pour diffuser leurs messages. Des groupes comme les fans de K-Pop ont utilisé ces plateformes pour soutenir des causes et même participer à des manifestations dans la rue. Cependant, tout le monde n'a pas un bon accès à Internet, et certains participent uniquement en ligne car c'est plus sûr et plus facile.

**Impact** – L'activisme en ligne permet de toucher beaucoup de personnes, notamment les jeunes qui ne participeraient pas forcément aux manifestations dans la rue. Il diffuse rapidement les idées et connecte différents groupes dans le monde. Mais l'accès inégal à Internet et les « chambres d'écho » en ligne limitent qui peut participer et combien de temps ils restent engagés. Cela montre que les manifestations en ligne ne suffisent pas seules, mais peuvent soutenir et développer les actions sur le terrain.

**Prochaine étape** – Les organisations sociales comptent combiner manifestations en ligne et hors ligne. Elles veulent garder l'intérêt des gens sur Internet et les aider à participer aussi dans la rue. Elles cherchent aussi à toucher ceux qui ont peu d'accès à Internet grâce à des rencontres en personne. Cette approche mixte peut rendre les mouvements plus forts et durables.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les manifestations en ligne offrent de nouvelles façons de s’engager, et combinées aux actions en personne, elles aident à créer des mouvements plus grands et durables dans le monde entier.
articles.personality_title_es: Cómo el activismo en línea está cambiando las protestas en el mundo
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Antes, las protestas ocurrían principalmente en las calles con gritos y pancartas. Pero ahora, gracias a las redes sociales, muchas protestas pasan en línea usando hashtags, videos y carteles digitales. Movimientos como la Primavera Árabe y Occupy mostraron cómo las acciones en línea pueden llevar a protestas en la vida real.

**Qué pasó** – Los expertos dicen que las protestas en línea y fuera de línea funcionan de manera similar, solo que en lugares diferentes. Las protestas en línea usan tendencias populares como memes y hashtags para difundir mensajes. Grupos como los fans del K-Pop han usado plataformas en línea para apoyar causas y también salir a las calles. Sin embargo, no todos tienen buen acceso a internet y algunos solo participan en línea porque es más seguro y fácil.
